title: There's No Crying in Flag Design
beats: Classroom frame: states are students; homework was to design their flag
Five graded rules: simple, distinct at distance, <=3 colors, meaningful symbols, no words
Absolute rule: never write your name; a flag is not a name tag
Tier list S-F, plus a tier list inside F tier
Worst first: seal-on-blue template; copying makes everyone less distinct
Oregon's back side is better; California fails for writing its name, A-in-F
Dakotas: name = instant fail; suggestion to coordinate sister designs
Mississippi redesigned: a model of achievable improvement
Rapid seal-on-blue grading: Nebraska, Vermont, Maine
New Mexico S tier: simple, symbolic, landscape colors - the positive exemplar
More blue belles: NH, Connecticut, Michigan
Alaska: great symbolism but low contrast at distance - B tier
Missouri, Rhode Island, Commonwealths, Virginia, Ohio, Delaware
Wyoming: presenter loves it yet his own rule forces an F
Colorado's giant C counts as writing; Minnesota worst in Union
Alabama: simple shape, a lesson that less does more
Nevada's two words get an exception: 'Battle Born'
Maryland so hideous it's S tier
Tennessee: B on screen, A in the air - the blue bar handles wind
Washington, Hawaii, Oklahoma, Carolinas, New Jersey
Arizona A; New York's disappointment vs London's Union Jack ubiquity
Georgia, Texas A with pride bonus, Florida copying Alabama
Utah redesign A, but S because bees and bestagons; class dismissed

metrics.misconception: yes: that a seal or the state's name makes a good flag; refuted by repeated failing grades
metrics.brute_force: yes 1:42: grade all 50 one by one against the rubric
metrics.examples: 50 states; worst-first, punctuated by exemplars (New Mexico 4:39, Alabama 11:26) and edge cases (Nevada words, Tennessee wind)
metrics.ending: Utah as presenter's personal S tier via callback to bestagon video; school bell

principles.1: confirmed: 0:00 classroom and homework, tier lists 'because you are all so Internet'
principles.2: confirmed: five rules only, then reused 50 times; no other apparatus
principles.3: confirmed: the rubric and S-F tier interface become automatic through ~50 repetitions
principles.4: partly: classroom metaphor sustained throughout, never stepped out of into formal vexillology
principles.5: confirmed: states literally embodied as students who object, cry, carry redesigns
principles.7: confirmed: by mid-video viewer predicts F for any name-on-flag before the verdict
principles.8: confirmed: speech stays fast; novelty pacing done by slowing for exemplars (New Mexico, Alaska, Wyoming) and speeding through repeat failures
principles.9: confirmed: same rubric over every state
principles.10: not-observed: ordering is by narrative contrast, not by complexity
principles.11: confirmed: rubric installed in first 70 s before any grading
principles.12: partly: London/Union Jack 16:27, Greenland-Antarctica 3:37, DC, own bestagon video
principles.13: partly: rules are kid-simple; reasons given (wind, distance) but little expert depth

new_moves.name: new:rubric-then-grade
new_moves.what: Front-load a short graded rule list, then teach entirely by applying it to many real cases

new_moves.name: new:contrast-relief
new_moves.what: Insert a positive exemplar after a run of failures so the rule is seen satisfied

new_moves.name: new:rule-overrides-taste
new_moves.what: Presenter shows he must fail something he loves, proving the rule is binding

new_moves.name: new:nested-tier-list
new_moves.what: Two-axis grade (pass/fail tier x quality within) separates hard rule from soft quality

new_moves.name: new:edge-case-exception
new_moves.what: Explicitly grant exceptions to show rules serve purpose, not letter

theory: Grey teaches design judgment by installing a five-rule rubric in about 70 seconds and then applying it 50 times. The nested tier list separates a hard rule (no name) from soft quality. Ordering by narrative contrast rather than difficulty (failure runs broken by exemplars, then exceptions and a rule overriding the presenter's own taste) keeps the repetition from going flat. By the end the viewer is grading before he does.
velocity: Playbook 'rubric-then-grade': state 3-5 rules as an on-screen checklist, then run many cases with rule ticks animated per case
Orchestrator: after ~5 cases, have the learner give the verdict first and compare (commit-to-answer)
Scene builder: two-axis score display (hard-constraint pass/fail x quality) for any judgment task
Pacing: dwell on exemplars and edge cases, fast-forward repetitive failures; adapt by learner prediction accuracy
quote: There's no crying in flag design.
